newsitem.title: USA: Plaintiffs' lawyer attacks Simpson trial claims.
newsitem.headline: Plaintiffs' lawyer attacks Simpson trial claims.

text.p: Closings arguments ended on Tuesday in O.J. Simpson's civil trial with a plantiffs' lawyer imploring jurors to find the former football star responsible for the murders of his ex-wife and her friend.

Lowering his voice for dramatic effect, Daniel Petrocelli told the panel: "It is you, ladies and gentlemen, and only you ... who have the duty to decide once and for all who was responsible for the (lost) lives of these two human beings."
Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki was to give jurors a lengthy list of legal instructions on Tuesday before turning the case over to them for deliberations.

Simpson, who was acquitted in October 1995 in the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman, faced a wrongful-death civil suit brought by the victims' families, who are seeking substantial monetary damages.

In a display of courtroom theatre, Petrocelli accused Simpson's legal defence team of mocking the victims' families when his lead attorney, Robert Baker, said on Monday that it costs only $200 to file a lawsuit in California.

Waving $200 in bills at Simpson, Petrocelli said, "They want to speak about the deaths of these two dead people in terms of $200." Then, still holding the money, he walked towards Simpson and shouted, "Give my client back his son and we will march out of here in a heartbeat."

Describing Simpson's stormy relationship with his ex-wife, Petrocelli, who wrapped up the plaintiffs' rebuttal argument, said: "They had been at war with each other and she's found dead. Coincidence?"

He told jurors not to be concerned about Simpson's motive for the crime, saying: "People, sadly, have been killed in relationships from Day One. Revenge, love, hatred and jealousy -- the oldest things known to man."

Petrocelli accused Simpson of "audacity" for testifying that he had never struck his former wife, the mother of his two young children, when the jury had been shown a photograph of a bruised and battered Nicole Brown Simpson.
"Mothers of children get killed all the time, men beat mothers of children, men kill mothers of children," he said.

He also told the jury they should not be influenced by the defence argument that Simpson had no motive to kill his ex-wife. He noted that, unlike a criminal trial, it was not required in a civil case to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, just by a preponderance of evidence.
"Quite simply, is it more likely or not that he did it?" the attorney said, stressing that the jury has only to believe more than half the evidence points to Simpson as the killer.

"This is not a first-degree murder case, we don't have to prove Mr. Simpson planned this ... that he went there and waited, that it was premeditated," Petrocelli said. "The only thing we have to prove is that he did it, not why he did it. Only he knows why he did it."
"Did we prove it? Absolutely," he told the jury.

As the 4-month-old trial lurched toward an end, the morning session was delayed more than 90 minutes because of an apparent problem with two of the jurors. But when the panel finally filed into court there was no indication what had held things up and Fujisaki made no comment on the matter.

In testimony and closing arguments, Simpson's attorneys tried to show that evidence in the case was planted in order to frame him, that it was contaminated by sloppy laboratory work and that police bungled their investigation.

But another plaintiffs' lawyer, Tom Lambert, said earlier on Tuesday that DNA test results on blood evidence found at the murder scene where the victims were stabbed to death and at Simpson's mansion two miles (three km) away were "extremely significant evidence establishing the guilt of Mr. Simpson."

Lambert said the only DNA witness brought on by the defence, Dr. John Gerdes, had agreed that the test results were significant and had only questioned one blood spot at the murder scene as being possibly contaminated.
